claims.text: The target alloy is an AlMgₓTiSnZn lightweight high-entropy alloy with density below 6 g/cm³.
Melt spinning produces a metastable, supersaturated state in the target alloy.
The rapidly solidified target alloy initially has a homogeneous microstructure.
Isothermal aging at 250°C for 1–4 hours transforms the homogeneous metastable state into a bimodal microstructure.
The aged bimodal microstructure contains distinct Mg-rich intermetallic regions.
Mg diffusion during isothermal aging drives phase separation and formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates modifies local chemical potentials.
The evolved microstructural heterogeneity alters local galvanic interactions during corrosion.
The evolved microstructural heterogeneity alters oxide-scale nucleation and growth during high-temperature exposure.
Aging reduces localized corrosion currents relative to the as-quenched state.
Aging produces a more uniform and adherent high-temperature oxide scale than in the as-quenched state.
Uniformly distributed fine intermetallics can promote a protective surface film and high corrosion resistance.
Rapid non-equilibrium solidification can suppress completion of phase reactions and retain a high-temperature phase because diffusion time is insufficient.
The hypothesis is bounded to aging at 250°C for 1–4 hours in an inert or low-oxygen atmosphere.
Changing aging temperature, duration, or atmosphere may produce different phase-evolution pathways and property changes.
The quantitative relationships among aging duration, phase-separation extent, and corrosion and oxidation improvements are not established.

Failure of aged samples to show a statistically significant corrosion-current decrease and improved oxide-scale uniformity and adherence relative to the as-quenched control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
